lesson.title: One small step at a time: Euler's method

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the hatched drift between the straight steps and the faint exact curve shrink when you pick smaller step sizes for the capacitor's discharge.
interactive.title: The stepper
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in thirteen small screens. A 100 µF capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a 10 kΩ resistor. So τ = RC = 1 s. Its rule is dV/dt = −V ÷ 1, in volts and seconds. Voltage runs up the side, from 0 to 12 V. Time runs along the bottom, from 0 to 3 s. A faint slope field fills the plot. A faint exact curve, V = 12 e^(−t), runs through it. Euler's method walks on top. At each point it reads the arrow there. It walks straight along that arrow for one step, of size h. Then it reads again. So new value = old value + h × slope at the old value. The gap between the walk and the curve is the drift. It is hatched. Screen 1 starts a dot at 12 V. The arrow there slopes −12 V a second. The dot walks 0.5 s along it, down to 6 V. Screen 2 asks where the next 0.5 s step lands. The choices are 3 V, 0 V or 4.41 V. Screen 3 draws both steps and the curve. At 1 s the walk reads 3 V. The curve reads 4.41 V. The 1.41 V drift between them is hatched. Short tangent ticks sit along the first step. They show the curve easing off. The step keeps its starting slope. Screen 4 asks where 0.25 s steps have reached by 0.5 s. The choices are 6.75 V, 7.28 V or 6 V. Screen 5 offers a named choice of step size. The sizes are 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5 or 1 s. It opens on 0.5 s. Each step's starting arrow is drawn where the step begins. So you can see every step use the slope at its start. A table logs the value at 1 s for each step size chosen. The curve's 4.41 V sits beside it. The rows read 4.30, 4.18, 3.80, 3.00 and 0 V. Their drifts are 0.11, 0.23, 0.62, 1.41 and 4.41 V. As the steps shrink, the value at 1 s climbs towards 4.41 V. On a phone the table's columns wrap. Screen 6 gives the drift with 0.1 s steps, 0.23 V. It asks the drift with 0.05 s steps. The choices are about 0.11 V, about 0.23 V or about 0.06 V. The 0.05 s row stays hidden until he checks. Screen 7 widens the plot. Voltage now runs from −12 to 12 V, and time from 0 to 6 s. A named choice offers 1, 1.5 or 2 s steps. It opens on 1.5 s. A dashed line marks the steady state at 0 V. Each step adds h × (−V ÷ τ). So each step multiplies the value by 1 − h ÷ τ. With 1 s steps the walk drops to 0 V at 1 s and stays there. With 1.5 s steps it goes 12, −6, 3, −1.5 and 0.75 V. It swings either side of 0 V and dies away. With 2 s steps it goes 12, −12, 12 and −12 V, for ever. The curve itself never crosses 0 V. Screen 8 asks where the first 1.5 s step from 12 V lands. The choices are −6 V, 0 V or 2.68 V. Screen 9 swaps in a tank. Its level y obeys dy/dt = 0.3 − 0.2 √y, in metres and minutes. It fills from empty. Level runs up the side, from 0 to 2.5 m. Time runs along the bottom, from 0 to 20 min. A dashed line marks the steady level, 2.25 m. There is no faint curve this time. This rule has no tidy formula for y against time. A named choice offers steps of 2, 1, 0.5 or 0.25 min. Each walk is drawn on top of the others. Readouts log the level at 4 min: 0.89, 0.79, 0.75 and 0.73 m. Each halving moves the answer less. Screen 10 asks where one 1 min step from 1 m lands. The choices are 1.1 m, 1.3 m or 0.1 m. Screens 11 to 13 mix everything together. Screen 11 steps the coil from the last lesson. Its rule is di/dt = (24 − 10 i) ÷ 0.5. It starts from 0 A and takes two steps of 0.01 s. The choices are 0.864 A, 0.96 A or 0.791 A. Screen 12 steps the same coil with 0.075 s steps. Its current reads 0, 3.6, 1.8 and 2.7 A. It asks why the current swings. One answer is that the step is longer than τ, so it overshoots. Another is that the current really rings. The third is that the steady value is 3.6 A. Screen 13 shows the tank at 4 min. It reads 0.79 m with 1 min steps and 0.75 m with 0.5 min steps. It asks what to do next. The choices are to halve the step again and compare, to take 0.79 m, or to average them to 0.77 m. Each puzzle offers three answers.
interactive.ignores: The steps are drawn slowly. They are also much larger than a computer would take. A computer also rounds each number a little. That rounding is left out here. The capacitor and resistor are ideal. The tank's rule is an example. Its outflow grows as the square root of the level. A real tank's outflow depends on its outlet. Euler's method is the simplest stepper. Better steppers read the slope more than once in each step.

explain.text:
Euler's method solves a rule by walking it. Stand at the start. Read the slope the rule gives there. Walk a short straight step along it. Then read the slope again where you land, and repeat.[^1] It needs no formula, only the rule. So it works even on rules that have no formula.

Take the 100 µF capacitor from before, now discharging through 10 kΩ. So τ = RC = 1 s. Its rule is dV/dt = −V ÷ 1. At 12 V the slope is −12 V a second. Walk 0.5 s along it and you fall 6 V. That lands you at 6 V. At 6 V the slope is −6 V a second. So the next 0.5 s takes you to 3 V. Each step is new value = old value + h × slope. Here h is the [[step size]]. That is [[Euler's method]].

The walk drifts from the true answer. At 1 s the exact curve reads 4.41 V. The walk reads only 3 V. The cause is in each step. A step keeps the slope it read at its start. Along the step the voltage falls. So the true slope eases off. The straight line does not. So the step falls too far. The walk drifts below the curve. Shorter steps re-read the slope more often. So a smaller step gives a better answer, and a larger step a worse one.[^2] At 1 s, 0.1 s steps give 4.18 V. Steps of 0.05 s give 4.30 V. For small steps the drift is about in proportion to the step. So halving the step roughly halved it.

Too big a step does worse than drift. Each step adds h × (−V ÷ τ) to V. So each step multiplies the voltage by 1 − h ÷ τ. With 1.5 s steps that factor is −0.5. The first step reads −12 V a second. It walks that slope for 1.5 s. It falls 18 V, straight past 0 V to −6 V. Then it swings back. The real voltage never goes below 0 V. So the swing comes only from the steps. With 2 s steps it swings for ever. In rules like these, the rate depends only on the value. Then the true curve can never cross its steady line. A walk that swings across that line is taking steps that are too big.

The same walk works where no tidy formula exists. Take a tank filled at a steady rate. It drains through its base. Its outflow grows with the square root of the depth. Say its level y obeys dy/dt = 0.3 − 0.2 √y, in metres and minutes. Its steady level is where inflow and outflow balance, at 2.25 m. You cannot rearrange this rule into a tidy formula for y against time. So step it. Then halve the step and step again. From empty, the level at 4 min reads 0.89 m with 2 min steps. As the steps halve, it reads 0.79 m, then 0.75 m, then 0.73 m. Each halving moves the answer less. When it barely moves, you can trust it.

**Euler's method walks short straight steps along the rule's slope, re-reading it after each one. Smaller steps drift less from the true curve. For a decay, steps longer than the time constant overshoot.**

analogy.text: Euler's method is dead reckoning. You know the boat's position, course and speed. Hold that course for a set time. Then mark the new position. Take the new course and speed, and run again. Long runs between updates drift further from the true track.
analogy.breaks: A navigator's course is set by the helm, not by where the boat is. Euler's slope changes with the value itself. A navigator also gets fixes that reset the error. Euler's method never gets a fix. Only short steps keep its drift small.

practice.text:
- Write the rule as slope = f(value, time).
- Choose a step size h. For a decay, start well under the time constant.
- Find the slope at the start.
- New value = old value + h × slope. New time = old time + h.
- Find the slope at the new value, and repeat.
- Halve h and run it again. If the answer barely moves, trust it.

**Rules of thumb:** here, steps of a tenth of τ left the value at one τ about 5% low. For a decay, steps longer than τ overshoot the steady state. A spreadsheet does this well. Give each step one row. Halving h doubles the rows, so smaller steps cost more work. A close cousin of this method works out how fast a submarine dives as its ballast tanks flood.[^3]

**Worked example:** take the coil from before. Its rule is di/dt = (24 − 10 i) ÷ 0.5, and it starts at 0 A. Use steps of 0.01 s. The starting slope is 24 ÷ 0.5 = 48 A a second. So after 0.01 s, i = 0 + 0.01 × 48 = 0.48 A. The slope there is (24 − 4.8) ÷ 0.5 = 38.4 A a second. So after 0.02 s, i = 0.48 + 0.384 = 0.864 A. The exact formula gives 0.791 A. The walk runs high. This curve flattens as it rises, but each step keeps its steeper starting slope.

**Common mistakes**
- Reusing the starting slope for every step. Re-read it at each new value.
- Expecting the steps to land on the exact curve. They drift from it. The drift builds up.
- Adding the slope instead of h × slope.
- Trusting a walk that swings across its steady line. When the rate depends only on the value, the true curve never crosses it. Shrink the step.
- Trusting one run. Halve the step and compare.

A 100 µF capacitor charged to 12 V discharges through a 10 kΩ resistor. Every value is an example.

Every step, drift and reading is worked out from the rule on its screen.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the hatched drift between the straight steps and the faint exact curve shrink when you pick smaller step sizes for the capacitor's discharge.

checks.label: Every step of every walk drawn heads along the rule's slope at its start, each step of a walk is the same length in time, and every slope arrow matches the rule where it is drawn

A smaller h would result in a better approximation, and a larger h in a worse one: the drift at one second shrinks with every smaller step size, and each halving of the tank's step moves its level at four minutes less than the halving before

Every worked number is right: 6 and 3 V after 0.5 s steps, 4.41 V exact and 1.41 V of drift at 1 s; 9 and 6.75 V after 0.25 s steps against 7.28 V; the log 0, 3.00, 3.80, 4.18 and 4.30 V with drifts 4.41, 1.41, 0.62, 0.23 and 0.11 V, 0.06 V for the quartered slip and 5% low at 0.1 s; 12, −6, 3, −1.5 and 0.75 V with 1.5 s steps, 12, −12, 12 and −12 V with 2 s steps, 0 V after one 1 s step, 2.68 V exact at 1.5 s and an 18 V fall; the tank steady at 2.25 m, 0.89, 0.79, 0.75 and 0.73 m at 4 min, 1.1 m after one step from 1 m, 1.3 m for the slip and 0.77 m for the average; the coil 48 and 38.4 A a second, 0.48 and 0.864 A, 0.96 A for the slip, 0.791 A exact, τ 0.05 s, steady 2.4 A, and 3.6, 1.8 and 2.7 A with 0.075 s steps

The capacitor's walks never rise above the exact curve, the coil's two small steps run above its curve, the exact curves never cross their steady lines, and only the 1.5 s and 2 s walks swing below 0 V

The log lists the value at 1 s and its drift for each step size tried, beside the exact 4.41 V; the halving puzzle shows the 0.05 s row only once it is answered; the tank's log lists its level at 4 min for each step tried
Each puzzle accepts only its answer, draws it when it is checked, and draws every wrong pick as a mistake
Before Check, no puzzle's picture shows its answer or a mistake
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, finishes within 2 s

applied.problem: The mistake "trusting a walk that swings either side of its steady line" is read alone for months; after i6 a lightly damped spring or circuit truly rings either side of its steady line, so the swing is only a warning sign when the rate depends only on the value.

"Where no formula exists" overstates the tank: dh/dt = 0.3 − 0.2 √h separates, giving time as a formula in the level; only the level against time has no tidy formula, as the next sentences rightly say.
"This rule has no tidy formula" is too broad: separating it gives time against level in closed form; what it lacks is a tidy formula for h against time, which is why no exact curve is drawn.
